how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture documentation showing an inline gateway with active content inspection policy; if no such gateway exists or it is in monitoring-only mode, set value to false.

typical_values: false (common — most broker deployments lack inline content inspection)
true (compliant — dedicated message security gateway or validation plugin active)

option_description: Indicates whether the message broker or middleware endpoint at the application tier boundary requires and validates the identity of all message producers before accepting messages. Authentication mechanisms include SASL (PLAIN, SCRAM, GSSAPI/Kerberos), mutual TLS (mTLS) with client certificates, or token-based authentication, with anonymous/unauthenticated producer connections explicitly rejected.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Zone Boundary Bypass Via Allowed Middleware Protocols' when both middleware_content_inspection_enabled and middleware_sender_authentication_enforced are false, and also fires independently when the middleware is exposed in 'external' or 'dmz' zones without sender authentication. Without sender authentication, any host with network access to broker ports can inject arbitrary messages (T1071.005, T1071), enabling zone boundary traversal through trusted protocol channels and potentially triggering malicious processing by backend consumers. Combined with external/DMZ exposure, unauthenticated brokers are directly exploitable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the RabbitMQ configuration to verify that the default guest user is disabled, SASL mechanisms require authentication, and anonymous connections are rejected. Also check whether TLS client certificate verification is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing 'auth_mechanisms.1 = PLAIN' with non-guest credentials and 'ssl_options.verify = verify_peer' with 'ssl_options.fail_if_no_peer_cert = true' confirm mTLS enforcement. Presence of 'default_user = guest' accessible from non-loopback addresses indicates authentication is NOT enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an anonymous or unauthenticated AMQP connection to the broker from an application tier host to verify whether the broker rejects unauthenticated producers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An 'ACCESS_REFUSED' or 'NOT_ALLOWED' exception indicates authentication is enforced. A successful connection with empty credentials confirms authentication is NOT enforced and the value should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Apache Kafka deployments used as JMS-compatible brokers, review the server.properties file for SASL or mTLS listener configuration to confirm client authentication is required.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries showing 'ssl.client.auth=required' and SASL_SSL listeners confirm authentication enforcement. 'PLAINTEXT' listeners or 'ssl.client.auth=none' indicates unauthenticated access is permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Azure Service Bus portal, verify that Shared Access Signature (SAS) policies or Azure AD authentication is required and that public network access without authentication is disabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Service Bus Namespace > [namespace] > Settings > Shared Access Policies; confirm no policies grant SendListen without token requirement; also check Networking > disable public network access if applicable
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All SAS policies require a valid token; 'Local Authentication' is not set to disabled without a compensating AD auth policy. Absence of any authentication requirement confirms false.

typical_values: false (common in internal-only broker deployments that rely solely on network-level access control)
true (compliant — SASL or mTLS enforced, anonymous connections rejected)

option_description: Classifies which network zone has reachability to AMQP (ports 5672/5671) or JMS broker ports. The three possible values reflect whether the broker is reachable from 'external' networks (internet-facing), the 'dmz' (semi-trusted perimeter zone), or only 'internal' application tier networks (most restrictive). This is determined by reviewing firewall rules, network ACLs, security group bindings, and broker listener interface bindings.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute to escalate risk: when middleware_protocol_exposure_zone is 'external' or 'dmz', the 'Zone Boundary Bypass Via Allowed Middleware Protocols' exposure fires independently for each missing control (sender authentication absent OR content inspection absent). Exposure in the DMZ or externally means broker ports are reachable from lower-trust networks, dramatically increasing the attack surface for T1071.005 (Publish/Subscribe Protocol abuse) and T1071 (Application Layer Protocol). Internal-only exposure limits the attack surface to already-compromised internal hosts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On AWS, identify which subnets the broker is deployed in and determine whether those subnets have routes to an internet gateway or are accessible from DMZ subnets via security group rules.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters 'Name=private-ip-address,Values=<broker-ip>' --query 'NetworkInterfaces[*].{SubnetId:SubnetId,SGs:Groups[*].GroupId,VpcId:VpcId}' --output json && aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters 'Name=association.subnet-id,Values=<broker-subnet-id>' --query 'RouteTables[*].Routes' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Route table showing only local VPC routes and no internet gateway route confirms internal zone. An IGW route or peering to a DMZ VPC indicates dmz or external exposure. Cross-reference security group rules for ports 5671-5672.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a port scan from a DMZ or external vantage point to confirm whether AMQP ports are reachable from outside the internal application tier.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ports shown as 'filtered' or 'closed' from a DMZ/external host confirm internal-only exposure. Ports shown as 'open' from DMZ or external networks indicate dmz or external zone value respectively.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the broker's listener binding configuration to determine which network interfaces and addresses AMQP listeners are bound to, confirming whether they are bound to internal-only or all interfaces.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Listener bound to a private RFC1918 IP address confirms internal exposure. Listener bound to '0.0.0.0' or a public IP requires further firewall review to determine actual zone reachability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the cloud console, review the security group or firewall rules associated with the broker instances and identify whether source CIDRs for ports 5671/5672 include external IP ranges, DMZ subnet CIDRs, or only application-tier internal CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Security Groups > [broker SG] > Inbound Rules > filter by Port 5671 or 5672; Azure Portal > Network Security Groups > [broker NSG] > Inbound Security Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source restricted to application-tier CIDR only = internal. Source includes DMZ CIDR = dmz. Source includes 0.0.0.0/0 or internet-routable CIDR = external.

typical_values: dmz (elevated risk — common in poorly segmented architectures)

option_description: Indicates whether all redundant and failover network paths — including load balancer secondary backends, active-passive NIC failover interfaces, BGP failover routes, and backup connectivity circuits — have firewall rules, ACLs, and security group policies that are identical or functionally equivalent to those applied on the primary boundary enforcement path. A value of false means at least one redundant path lacks policy parity with the primary path.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Inconsistent Boundary Enforcement Across Redundant Paths' exposure when failover_paths_policy_parity is false (checked via 'not input.failover_paths_policy_parity'). Asymmetric policy application on failover paths creates exploitable gaps (T1599 — Network Boundary Bridging) that adversaries can abuse during or by inducing failover events. Failover paths with weaker policies become fallback channels (T1008) for C2 or lateral movement that would be blocked on the primary path. This is particularly dangerous because failover conditions are often not monitored as closely as steady-state operations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On AWS, enumerate all security groups associated with both primary and failover/secondary ENIs of application tier load balancers and instances, then compare inbound and outbound rule sets for differences.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing all ENIs and their associated security groups; if primary ENI security groups differ from secondary ENI security groups, parity is absent. Identical security group IDs across all ENIs indicates parity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For on-premises environments with multiple uplinks or VLAN interfaces, compare iptables rule counts and key rules between the primary and secondary/failover network interfaces on application tier hosts.
how_to_obtain.command: for iface in $(ip link show | awk -F': ' '/^[0-9]+:/{print $2}' | grep -v lo); do echo "=== $iface ==="; iptables -L -n --line-numbers | grep $iface 2>/dev/null || iptables -L -n --line-numbers; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Identical rule sets across all interfaces indicate parity. Differences in ACCEPT/DROP rules between primary and secondary interfaces confirm policy disparity and a false value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform, CloudFormation, or Ansible infrastructure-as-code for the application tier to verify that security group attachments and ACL associations are explicitly applied to all failover and secondary network resources, not just primary ones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IaC files showing security_group_ids or network_acl_id references for both primary and failover resources with matching policy IDs confirm parity. Missing security references on failover resources indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, navigate to EC2 > Load Balancers, select the application tier ALB or NLB, review the security groups and target group health checks for both primary and failover target groups, then verify that backend security groups are consistent.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > [app-tier LB] > Security tab (SGs on LB) and Description tab (target groups); then EC2 > Target Groups > [each TG] > Targets tab > verify each target instance uses identical security groups
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All target instances and load balancer ENIs associated with identical security group sets confirms parity. Any instance using a different security group on a failover path indicates false.

typical_values: true (compliant — policy parity verified across all paths)
false (common finding — failover interfaces provisioned without replicating primary policy)
null (not assessed — redundant paths not inventoried)

option_description: Indicates whether deep packet inspection (DPI), IDS/IPS sensors, or equivalent traffic analysis tools are actively applied to redundant and failover network paths — including secondary NICs, backup WAN circuits, and failover routes — and not only to the primary network path. This requires that inspection appliances either receive mirrored traffic from all paths or are inline on all paths including failover.
security_impact: The Rego policy independently triggers 'Inconsistent Boundary Enforcement Across Redundant Paths' exposure when redundant_path_inspection_enabled is false (checked via 'not input.redundant_path_inspection_enabled'). Without inspection on redundant paths, adversaries can route traffic through failover interfaces to evade IDS/IPS monitoring (T1599 — Network Boundary Bridging), establish fallback C2 channels (T1008) through uninspected secondary routes, and conduct lateral movement or exfiltration during failover events when only the primary path is monitored. The monitoring gap compounds the risk of policy parity issues.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On AWS, verify that VPC Traffic Mirroring sessions are configured to capture traffic from all ENIs on application tier instances, including secondary/failover ENIs, not just the primary ENI.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-traffic-mirror-sessions --query 'TrafficMirrorSessions[*].{SessionID:TrafficMirrorSessionId,SourceENI:NetworkInterfaceId,TargetID:TrafficMirrorTargetId,Filter:TrafficMirrorFilterId}' --output json && aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters 'Name=attachment.instance-id,Values=<instance-id>' --query 'NetworkInterfaces[*].{ENI:NetworkInterfaceId,Device:Attachment.DeviceIndex}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cross-referencing traffic mirror sessions against all ENIs on app tier instances; every ENI (DeviceIndex 0, 1, 2...) should appear as a SourceENI in a mirror session. Any ENI not appearing in mirror sessions confirms inspection is absent on that path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review IDS/IPS sensor deployment configuration (e.g., Snort, Suricata) to verify that sensor interface listening configuration includes all physical or virtual interfaces, including failover interfaces.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML entries listing multiple interface names (e.g., eth0, eth1, bond1) under the af-packet or pcap section confirm multi-path inspection. Only a single interface listed indicates secondary paths are not inspected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network security team to obtain the IDS/IPS sensor placement topology diagram and verify that tap or span points exist on all redundant and failover paths, not just the primary perimeter path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture diagram showing span/tap points on each redundant circuit or failover interface with confirmed IDS/IPS processing. Diagrams showing inspection only on primary path confirm redundant_path_inspection_enabled is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Trigger or simulate a failover event, then generate known IDS/IPS test traffic (e.g., EICAR test string over HTTP) through the failover path and confirm whether the IDS/IPS generates an alert, verifying that the failover path is under active inspection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An IDS/IPS alert generated and visible in the SIEM or sensor console within 60 seconds of sending test traffic over the failover path confirms inspection is active. No alert generated confirms redundant_path_inspection_enabled is false.

typical_values: false (common — IDS/IPS deployed only on primary path, failover paths overlooked)
true (compliant — all paths including failover covered by inspection)

option_description: Indicates whether boundary crossing events — specifically network traffic transiting the application tier boundary — are captured in logs when that traffic flows through redundant or failover network paths, providing complete audit trail parity between primary and failover path logging. This requires that firewall logs, flow logs (e.g., VPC Flow Logs, NetFlow), or equivalent telemetry from failover interfaces are forwarded to the central logging system.
security_impact: The Rego policy independently triggers 'Inconsistent Boundary Enforcement Across Redundant Paths' exposure when failover_boundary_crossing_logged is false (checked via 'not input.failover_boundary_crossing_logged'). This has criticality 'low' with a score of 2, but it is a foundational forensic requirement: without logging on failover paths, adversaries exploiting fallback channels (T1008) or performing network boundary bridging (T1599) during failover events leave no audit trail, preventing incident detection, investigation, and response. Logging gaps on failover paths are particularly exploitable because failover events are often treated as operational incidents rather than security events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On AWS, verify that VPC Flow Logs are enabled at the VPC or subnet level for the application tier and that they cover all traffic (ACCEPT and REJECT). Then confirm that the Flow Log covers all ENIs including secondary/failover ENIs by checking the resource-level scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flow logs with TrafficType=ALL and Status=ACTIVE covering the application tier VPC ID confirm logging is enabled. LogDestinationType should be cloud-watch-logs or s3 (with confirmed delivery). If no flow logs are returned, logging is absent and value is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Simulate a failover event and then query the central SIEM or log aggregation system for flow log entries originating from the failover interface IP or subnet CIDR within the failover window to confirm log delivery from the secondary path.
how_to_obtain.command: aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name '/aws/vpc/flowlogs/app-tier' --start-time $(date -d '30 minutes ago' +%s000) --filter-pattern '"<failover-interface-ip>"' --query 'events[*].{Timestamp:timestamp,Message:message}' --output json | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing srcaddr or dstaddr matching the failover interface IP during the simulated failover window confirm logging is active on that path. Zero results despite confirmed failover traffic indicates logging is absent and value is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS CloudWatch or Azure Monitor console, navigate to the flow logs or Network Watcher logs for the application tier, filter by the failover subnet or secondary NIC, and verify that log entries are present and current.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > CloudWatch > Log Groups > [VPC Flow Log group] > Log Streams > search for stream matching failover ENI ID; OR Azure Portal > Monitor > Network > Network Watcher > NSG Flow Logs > [failover subnet NSG] > verify storage account has recent log files
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active log streams with recent entries (within last 24 hours) for failover path ENIs or subnets confirm logging is enabled. Missing log streams or empty/stale log groups confirm false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM ingestion configuration and log source inventory to verify that failover path logging sources (secondary ENI flow logs, backup circuit NetFlow exporters, or standby firewall log streams) are explicitly listed as active ingestion sources.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SIEM log source inventory showing explicit entries for failover interface flow logs or NetFlow sources with recent last-seen timestamps confirms logging parity. Absence of failover path sources in the SIEM inventory confirms false.

typical_values: false (common — flow logs enabled only on primary subnets, failover subnets omitted)
true (compliant — all paths including failover captured in centralized logging)
null (not assessed — failover path logging coverage not verified)
